title: The Step-Cost Blind Spot: Why Growth Alone Doesn't Lift Your Margin
linkedin:
Six weeks into the new financial year, most business owners are pulling their first real comparison against last year. Revenue is often up. Margin often isn't moving the way that revenue suggests it should.

It's rarely one bad decision. It's usually a cost that jumped once: a second vehicle leased, a supervisor role added, a bigger premises taken on before the volume was really there to fill it.

None of those calls were wrong. Each one just moved the cost base up a level that revenue hasn't caught up to yet.

Here's the part that catches most owners out. Gross margin percentage is often the last place this shows up clearly, because revenue is climbing at the same time the cost base jumped. The percentage looks roughly steady while the dollar cost of running the business at this new size has moved meaningfully underneath it.

The more reliable read isn't the percentage. It's cost per job, per client, per delivery run, tracked against the same measure from before the step was taken.

None of this means step costs are wrong to take. Businesses that never add capacity eventually hit a ceiling they can't trade past. The difference between a step that builds the business and one that quietly erodes a year of trading is whether anyone set a revenue marker for it, and whether anyone checks the numbers against that marker every month.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog. Link in the first comment.

More often it's a cost that jumped once: a second vehicle, an extra shift, a bigger premises, taken on before the trading volume caught up to it. None of these are the wrong calls to make.
